topics.name: Billy the Kid - Play Study
facts: Billy the Kid is a powerful play that explores themes of war, loss, memory, and identity.
The play follows the life of Billy, who dreams of being a footballer but is drawn into the Second World War.
A key theme of the play is war and its effects.
Another key theme is memory and nostalgia.
The play also explores growing up and responsibility.
Friendship and loss are major themes in Billy the Kid.
The setting of the play is during the Second World War.
Billy's dream before the war is to be a footballer.
A key question to consider is: What was the message or moral of the play?
The play uses staging, lighting, sound, and acting to communicate its themes.

retrieval_questions.q: What is Billy the Kid about?
retrieval_questions.a: A play exploring war, loss, memory, and identity, following Billy who dreams of being a footballer but is drawn into the Second World War.

retrieval_questions.a: A footballer.

retrieval_questions.q: Which war is Billy drawn into?
retrieval_questions.a: The Second World War.

retrieval_questions.q: Name two key themes of Billy the Kid.
retrieval_questions.a: War and its effects; memory and nostalgia (also growing up and responsibility; friendship and loss).

retrieval_questions.a: Memory and nostalgia.

retrieval_questions.a: Growing up and responsibility.

retrieval_questions.a: What was the message or moral of the play?

retrieval_questions.a: Loss (of friends, of innocence, of identity).

retrieval_questions.q: What theme connects characters in Billy the Kid through their relationships?
retrieval_questions.a: Friendship and loss.

retrieval_questions.q: What sort of play is Billy the Kid described as?
retrieval_questions.a: A powerful play exploring themes of war, loss, memory, and identity.

topics.name: Theatre Review Structure
facts: A theatre review should have three key sections: Introduction, Main Body, and Conclusion.
The Introduction states what the play was called, where and when you saw it, who performed it, and what it was about.
The Main Body discusses Acting, Set/Costume, Lighting & Sound, and memorable Moments.
When reviewing acting, you should consider whether it was believable and who stood out.
When reviewing Set/Costume, you should consider how the design helped tell the story.
When reviewing Lighting & Sound, you should consider whether they were effective in creating mood or atmosphere.
You should pick 1-2 scenes and explain what made them memorable.
The Conclusion explains what you enjoyed most and why, and whether you would recommend it and to whom.
Sentence starters to describe a moment include: 'The moment that stood out was when...', 'This was effective because...', 'The actor used [gesture/voice/facial expression] to show...'.
Sentence starters to evaluate performance include: 'The performance made me feel... because...', 'The actor successfully showed [emotion/character] by...', 'The lighting helped create...'.
A practice task asks: What happened in the scene? How did the actor use voice/body to show emotion? How did lighting/sound/costume help? What effect did it have on the audience?

retrieval_questions.q: What are the three key sections of a theatre review?
retrieval_questions.a: Introduction, Main Body, and Conclusion.

retrieval_questions.q: What four things should the Introduction of a theatre review include?
retrieval_questions.a: What the play was called, where and when you saw it, who performed it, and what it was about.

retrieval_questions.q: What four areas are covered in the Main Body of a theatre review?
retrieval_questions.a: Acting, Set/Costume, Lighting & Sound, and memorable Moments.

retrieval_questions.q: What two questions should you ask about acting in a review?
retrieval_questions.a: Was it believable? Who stood out?

retrieval_questions.q: What should you consider when reviewing Set/Costume?
retrieval_questions.a: How the design helped tell the story.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the purpose of considering Lighting & Sound in a review?
retrieval_questions.a: To evaluate whether they were effective in creating mood or atmosphere.

retrieval_questions.q: How many memorable scenes/moments should you pick to discuss?
retrieval_questions.a: 1-2 scenes.

retrieval_questions.q: What two things does the Conclusion address?
retrieval_questions.a: What you enjoyed most and why, and whether you would recommend it and to whom.

retrieval_questions.q: Give a sentence starter for describing a memorable moment.
retrieval_questions.a: 'The moment that stood out was when...' or 'This was effective because...'.

retrieval_questions.q: Give a sentence starter for evaluating performance.
retrieval_questions.a: 'The performance made me feel... because...' or 'The actor successfully showed [emotion/character] by...'.

retrieval_questions.q: What four questions does the practice task ask about a moment?
retrieval_questions.a: What happened in the scene? How did the actor use voice/body to show emotion? How did lighting/sound/costume help? What effect did it have on the audience?

retrieval_questions.q: What aspect of audience experience should a review consider?
retrieval_questions.a: The effect a scene or performance had on the audience (mood, atmosphere, feeling).

topics.name: Key Drama Vocabulary
facts: Gesture is a movement made with the hand, arm, or head to express an idea or feeling.
Expression is the look on someone's face showing emotion.
Projection is speaking loudly and clearly so the audience can hear.
Ensemble is a group of actors working together on stage.
Atmosphere is the feeling or mood created by the performance.
Characterisation is the way an actor shows a character's personality.
Symbolism is using props, costumes or actions to represent deeper ideas.
Staging is how the stage space is used.
These key terms help you describe and evaluate performance in a theatre review.
A skills knowledge organiser can be used alongside this vocabulary to retrieve definitions and examples.
